intro: About 900 years ago, a few knights in Jerusalem made a promise. They would guard travelers on dangerous roads. They would also live like monks. People called them the Knights Templar. In time, they grew rich and famous across Europe.

Then, one Friday morning in 1307, the king of France had them arrested. Their story ended in trials, a lost parchment and many legends. Some legends are still told today, about treasure, curses and secret survival.

In this unit, you will learn how the Templars lived and why they fell. You will read real records from the time. You will practice a skill historians use every day: sorting what the evidence shows from what a story only claims.
bigQuestion: How can we tell what really happened to the Knights Templar from the legends people tell about them?

timeline.t: Christian armies from Europe take Jerusalem in the First Crusade.
Hugh of Payns and a few knights begin guarding pilgrims in Jerusalem.
The Council of Troyes gives the Templars their written Rule.
The Temple Church in London is blessed.
Acre falls, and the Templars lose their main home in the Holy Land.
On Friday, 13 October, King Philip IV has the Templars in France arrested.
Three cardinals forgive Templar leaders at Chinon Castle.
Pope Clement V ends the Templar order without a guilty verdict.
Jacques de Molay, the last Grand Master, is put to death in Paris.
American Masonic Knights Templar, inspired by the old order, meet in Chicago.
Barbara Frale finds the misfiled Chinon Parchment in the Vatican's archive.

a group of people who live by the same religious rules and promises
a written set of rules for how members of a religious order live

They made gold coins for Rome
test.why: The Templars kept money safe for people and helped move it over long distances.

By selling it to the king

They were inspired by the old order but not descended from it

write.prompt: Were the Templars guilty of the charges against them? Write a paragraph that answers the question. Use two or three facts or sources from this unit, such as the confessions, the Chinon Parchment or the pope's 1312 decision. Explain how each one supports your answer.
tips: Start with one clear sentence that gives your answer.
Name each source you use, like the Chinon Parchment.
Tell how the confessions were given before you trust them.
Say what someone who disagrees might point to.
Use unit words like charge, confess and evidence.

title: The Knights Templar

chapters.title: Monks Who Were Knights
chapters.bigQuestion: How did a small group of knights guarding pilgrims grow into one of the richest groups in Europe?

story.title: A Receipt for the Road
story.kicker: A traveler in France is scared to carry his money on a long trip. The knights next door have an idea.
paragraphs: It is a cold spring morning in France, about 850 years ago. A farmer we will call Pierre is packing for a long trip. He wants to walk to Jerusalem, a holy city far away. The trip may take many months. Pierre has saved coins for years to pay for food and boats on the way.

Pierre is worried. Robbers wait on the roads. A bag of coins is easy to steal. His neighbor tells him about the knights at the big stone house near the market. They wear white cloaks with red crosses. People say they keep money safe for travelers.

Pierre knocks on the heavy door. A brother in a plain cloak lets him in. Pierre sets his coins on a wooden table. The brother counts them slowly. Then he dips a feather pen in ink. He writes how much Pierre left on a small piece of parchment. He hands Pierre the written receipt.

Pierre folds the receipt and tucks it inside his shirt. Now he carries a piece of writing, not a heavy bag of gold. He walks out into the street feeling lighter. Pierre is a made-up person. But the knights and their money-keeping were real. Historians still study the records of how they did it.
story.think: Why might Pierre feel safer carrying a piece of paper than a bag of coins? What would he need to trust?

lessons.title: Pilgrims to Jerusalem
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1100s, many Christians walked to Jerusalem as pilgrims, and the roads there were dangerous.
reading: Jerusalem is a very old city. It is holy to Jews, Christians and Muslims. In 1099, Christian armies from Europe took the city in a war. These wars are called the *Crusades*. After that, more Christian travelers came from Europe to visit.
A *pilgrim* is a person who travels to a holy place to pray. Many pilgrims landed at a port by the sea. Then they walked inland to Jerusalem. The road ran through dry hills with few towns.
Robbers hid along these roads. They attacked travelers and took their things. Pilgrims had no one to protect them. Some people began to ask: who will keep the travelers safe?

words.d: a person who travels to a holy place to pray
wars in which armies from Europe fought to control Jerusalem and nearby lands, starting in 1096

look.title: A Road in Words
look.text: Picture a dusty road climbing through brown hills. The sun is hot. A small group of pilgrims walks slowly. One leads a donkey with bags. There are no houses in sight. Behind a big rock, someone is watching them.
look.prompt: What dangers do you see on this road? What would help these travelers feel safe?

check.q: What is a pilgrim?
choices: A soldier who guards a castle
A person who writes history books
A person who travels to a holy place to pray
check.why: The reading says a pilgrim travels to a holy place to pray.

check.q: Why were the roads to Jerusalem dangerous?
choices: The roads were covered in snow
Boats could not reach the city
check.why: The reading says robbers hid along the roads and attacked travelers.

check.q: Jerusalem is holy to which groups?
check.why: The reading says Jerusalem is holy to Jews, Christians and Muslims.

lessons.title: Hugh of Payns Starts a Brotherhood
lessons.mainIdea: About 1119 or 1120, a French knight named Hugh of Payns and a few friends promised to guard pilgrims.
reading: Hugh of Payns was a knight from France. About 1119 or 1120, he and a few other knights made a plan in Jerusalem. They would guard pilgrims on the roads. They would also live like monks, with prayer and simple lives.

They called themselves the Poor Fellow-Soldiers of Christ. King Baldwin II of Jerusalem gave them rooms in part of his palace. The palace stood on the Temple Mount. People then believed King Solomon's Temple had once stood there.

Because of that building, people called the knights the Templars. A *Templar* is a member of this order. An *order* is a group of people who live by the same religious rules. Their full name grew long: the Poor Fellow-Soldiers of Christ and of the Temple of Solomon.

words.d: a member of the Knights Templar, a religious order of knights begun about 1120
a group of people who live by the same religious rules and promises

look.title: How It Began
rows: Hugh of Payns and friends begin (about)
look.cite: Malcolm Barber, The New Knighthood: A History of the Order of the Temple (Cambridge University Press, 1994)
look.prompt: How many years after the Christians took Jerusalem did the Templars begin? Show how you figured it out.

check.q: Who was Hugh of Payns?
choices: A French knight who helped start the Templars
A robber on the pilgrim road
check.why: The reading says Hugh of Payns was a French knight who began the brotherhood with a few friends.

check.q: Why were the knights called Templars?
choices: They built a temple in France
They lived on the Temple Mount, where people thought Solomon's Temple had stood
check.why: The king gave them rooms on the Temple Mount, so people called them Templars.

check.q: What is an order?
choices: A group of people who live by the same religious rules
check.why: An order is a group of people who live by the same religious rules and promises.

lessons.title: Two Dates for One Beginning
lessons.mainIdea: An old writer said the Templars began in 1118, but most historians today think it was 1119 or 1120.
reading: William of Tyre was an archbishop who lived in the Holy Land. In the 1170s and 1180s, he wrote a long history of the kingdom of Jerusalem. He told how the Templars began. He said it happened in 1118.

But William wrote about 50 years after the start. He was not there. Historians today compare his book with other old records. Most of them think the Templars began in 1119 or early 1120. The start is *documented*, but the exact year is *disputed*.
William also said there were only nine knights for nine years. Other records show Hugh traveling in Europe to find new members by 1127. So many historians think the nine-knights story is too simple.

words.d: shown by records or objects from the time
argued about; experts do not all agree
a church leader in charge of other bishops in a region

look.title: William of Tyre Tells the Story
look.text: In the year 1118, some noble knights, loyal to God, promised to live in poverty and obey the church leader of Jerusalem. The king gave them a home in his palace near the Temple. For nine years they wore only clothes that people gave them.
look.cite: William of Tyre, History of Deeds Done Beyond the Sea, Book 12, chapter 7 (written c. 1170s-1180s)
look.prompt: William wrote about 50 years after 1118. Which part of his story would you want to check against other records? Why?

check.q: What year did William of Tyre give for the Templars' start?
check.why: William of Tyre wrote that the Templars began in 1118.

check.q: Why do historians question William's date?
choices: He never wrote about the Templars
He wrote about 50 years later and was not there
check.why: William wrote about 50 years after the start, so historians check him against other records.

check.q: What does disputed mean?
check.why: Disputed means experts argue about it and do not all agree.

lessons.title: A Rule to Live By
lessons.mainIdea: In about 1129, church leaders at Troyes, France, gave the Templars a written Rule of 72 parts.
reading: In about 1129, church leaders met in the town of Troyes, in France. Hugh of Payns came to ask for their help. The meeting is called the Council of Troyes. There, the Templars got a written *Rule*.

A Rule is a book of rules for how members of an order live. The Templars' first Rule was written in Latin. It had 72 short parts. Much of it was based on an older Rule for monks, the Rule of Saint Benedict.
A *monk* is a man who gives his life to God and lives by strict rules with other monks. Most monks prayed and worked quietly. The Templars were new. They were monks who also rode to battle.

words.d: a written set of rules for how members of a religious order live
a man who gives his life to God and lives by strict rules with other monks

look.title: A Rule Book You Know
look.text: Think of the rules posted in your classroom. One says to raise your hand. One says to walk in the hall. One says to put supplies back. Each rule helps the whole class work together. Now imagine a rule book with 72 rules for every part of your day.
look.prompt: Pick one classroom rule. What problem does it solve? What problem might a rule about meals or clothing solve for a group of knights?

check.q: Where did the Templars get their first written Rule?
choices: At the Council of Troyes in France
check.why: Church leaders at the Council of Troyes, in France, gave the Templars their Rule in about 1129.

check.q: How many parts did the first Templar Rule have?
check.why: The first Rule, written in Latin, had 72 short parts.

check.q: What made the Templars different from most monks?
choices: They were monks who also rode to battle
check.why: Most monks prayed and worked quietly. The Templars were monks who also fought.

lessons.title: Three Promises and Quiet Meals
lessons.mainIdea: Templars promised to own nothing of their own, not to marry, and to obey their leaders.
reading: When a man joined the Templars, he made three big promises. He would own nothing for himself. He would not marry. He would obey the leaders of the order. Promises like these are called vows. Each one is a *vow*.
The Rule filled each day with prayer. The brothers ate meals together in one hall. They were to eat quietly while someone read aloud. Their clothes were plain, with no fancy decorations.

Some rules were about knightly life. The Rule said how brothers should care for their horses. It also said the brothers must not go hunting for fun. The one animal they were allowed to hunt was the lion.

words.d: a serious promise, often made to God
a member of a religious order of men

look.title: From the Templar Rule
look.text: The brothers should eat together and keep quiet at the table while a holy book is read. Their clothes should be plain, with nothing just for show. They should not hunt birds or other animals for sport. Only the lion may be hunted.
look.cite: The Latin Rule of the Templars, Council of Troyes, c. 1129; English translation in J. M. Upton-Ward, The Rule of the Templars (Boydell, 1992)
look.prompt: Pick one rule. What do you think it was meant to teach the brothers about how to live?

check.q: What is a vow?
check.why: A vow is a serious promise, often made to God.

check.q: Which was one of the three Templar promises?
choices: To obey the leaders of the order
To live alone in the woods
check.why: Templars promised to own nothing, not to marry, and to obey their leaders.

check.q: Which animal did the Rule allow the brothers to hunt?
check.why: The Rule said the brothers must not hunt for fun, but the lion was allowed.

lessons.title: White Mantle, Red Cross
lessons.mainIdea: Templar knights wore a white mantle, later with a red cross, so everyone could see who they were.
reading: A *mantle* is a long cloak worn over other clothes. The Rule said the knights should wear white mantles. White stood for a clean, pure life. Other brothers wore black or brown.
In the 1140s, a pope allowed the Templars to add a red cross to their clothes. The red cross showed they would give their lives for their faith. Soon the white mantle with the red cross was famous.

The Templars also had a *seal*. A seal is a stamp pressed into wax to show who sent a letter. Their seal showed two knights riding on one horse. Many people think it stood for being poor and sharing. Historians still talk about its meaning.

words.d: a long, loose cloak worn over other clothes
a stamp pressed into wax to show who sent a letter
a picture or sign that stands for an idea

look.title: Two Knights, One Horse
look.text: Look closely at a round wax seal. In the middle, two knights sit on one horse. Both hold shields. Both hold long spears. The horse is walking forward. Words in Latin run around the edge of the circle.
look.prompt: Why might a group choose this picture as its symbol? Give one idea about what it could mean.

check.q: What is a mantle?
choices: A long cloak worn over other clothes
check.why: A mantle is a long, loose cloak worn over other clothes.

check.q: What color mantle did Templar knights wear?
check.why: The Rule said knights wore white mantles. Other brothers wore black or brown.

check.q: What did the Templar seal show?
check.why: The Templar seal showed two knights on one horse.

lessons.title: Gifts of Land
lessons.mainIdea: People across Europe gave the Templars land and money, so the order grew rich and set up houses in many countries.
reading: Many people in Europe admired the Templars. They wanted to help guard the pilgrims. So they gave gifts. Kings and nobles gave land, farms, mills and money. Some farmers gave a small field.

The Templars set up houses on this land. A Templar house that ran farms and land in one area is often called a *commandery*. Soon there were Templar houses in France, England, Spain, Portugal, Italy and other lands.
Most brothers in Europe were not fighters. Many ran farms. They sold crops and wool. They sent money and horses east to the knights in the Holy Land. The farms in Europe fed the fight far away.

words.d: a Templar house that ran farms and land in one area
a person from a rich, powerful family, often with land and a title

look.title: A Map in Words
look.text: Picture a map of Europe. Put a small dot for each Templar house. Dots fill France. Dots spread into England, Spain and Portugal. More dots appear in Italy and farther east. Now draw arrows from all the dots to one place: Jerusalem.
look.prompt: What do the arrows show? How did houses far from Jerusalem help the knights there?

check.q: Why did people give land to the Templars?
choices: The Templars bought all of it
The king made them sell it
They wanted to move to Jerusalem
They admired them and wanted to help guard pilgrims
check.why: The reading says people admired the Templars and wanted to help, so they gave gifts.

check.q: What is a commandery?
choices: A Templar house that ran farms and land in one area
check.why: A commandery was a Templar house that ran farms and land in one area.

check.q: What did most Templar brothers in Europe do?
choices: Ran farms and sent help east
check.why: Most brothers in Europe ran farms and sent money and horses to the Holy Land.

lessons.title: Keeping Money Safe
lessons.mainIdea: The Templars kept money safe and moved payments from place to place, an early kind of banking.
reading: The Templars had strong houses and trusted brothers. So people asked them to keep money safe. A person could leave coins or treasure at a Templar house. This is called a *deposit*. The Templars kept a record of it.

The Templars also helped move money over long distances. Their houses were in many countries. They could write down a payment in one place and settle it through another house. Historians call this a *transfer*. It is safer than carrying gold on a ship.

In time, even kings trusted them. The Templar house in Paris kept money for the kings of France. Historians call this an early kind of *banking*. Some popular books add more details. Historians are careful to say only what the old records show.

words.d: money or treasure left with someone to keep safe
moving money from one place or person to another
the work of keeping, lending and moving money for people

look.title: Coins or a Note?
look.text: Two travelers leave the same town. The first carries a heavy bag of coins. It clinks with every step. The second carries a folded note that says how much money she left at a Templar house. It fits in her sleeve.
look.prompt: Which traveler would a robber notice first? What must the second traveler trust for her plan to work?

check.q: What is a deposit?
choices: Money left with someone to keep safe
check.why: A deposit is money or treasure left with someone to keep safe.

check.q: Whose money did the Templar house in Paris keep?
check.why: The reading says the Paris Templar house kept money for the kings of France.

check.q: Why could the Templars move money over long distances?
choices: They had houses in many countries
check.why: Their houses in many countries let them settle a payment through another house.

lessons.title: Castles and Round Churches
lessons.mainIdea: The Templars built strong castles in the Holy Land and in Europe, and churches in many towns.
reading: In the Holy Land, the Templars guarded roads and borders. They built and held castles. One, near the sea at Atlit, was begun about 1218. It was called the Pilgrims' Castle. Its thick walls faced the water on three sides.
In Portugal, the Templars built a castle at Tomar, begun in 1160. It became their main house in that country. Its round church still stands today. Visitors can walk inside it.

In London, the Templars built the Temple Church. Its round part was blessed in 1185. Part of it is round. It was built to remind people of a famous round church in Jerusalem. You can still visit it. A *castle* guarded land. A church was for prayer. The Templars needed both.

words.d: a large, strong building with thick walls, built to protect people and land
the area around Jerusalem, holy to Jews, Christians and Muslims

look.title: Templar Buildings That Still Stand
look.cite: Helen Nicholson, The Knights Templar: A New History (Sutton, 2001)
look.prompt: Which building is the oldest? About how many years apart are the oldest and the newest?

check.q: What was the Templar castle at Atlit called?
check.why: The castle begun at Atlit about 1218 was called the Pilgrims' Castle.

check.q: Which Templar building is in London?
check.why: The Temple Church in London was blessed in 1185.

check.q: Why is part of the Temple Church round?
choices: To remind people of a round church in Jerusalem
check.why: The reading says it was built round to remind people of a famous round church in Jerusalem.

lessons.title: A Famous Monk Cheers Them On
lessons.mainIdea: Bernard of Clairvaux, a famous monk, wrote a letter praising the Templars as a new kind of knight.
reading: Bernard of Clairvaux was one of the most famous monks in Europe. People listened when he spoke. Hugh of Payns asked him for help. Around the 1130s, Bernard wrote to Hugh and his knights. His writing is called In Praise of the New Knighthood.

Bernard said the Templars were a new kind of knight. Ordinary knights often fought for money or pride. Bernard said Templars fought to protect others and lived simple, holy lives. He praised their plain clothes and their obedience.

Bernard's letter was a kind of *praise*. It helped the Templars find new members and gifts. When you read old writing, it helps to ask who wrote it and why. Bernard wanted people to support the new order. He was their *supporter*.

words.d: words that say good things about someone
a person who helps a group and speaks up for it

look.title: Bernard's New Knight
look.text: Bernard wrote that this new knight fights two battles at the same time. One battle is against enemies he can see. The other is against evil inside the heart. He said such a knight has no fear, because he trusts God.
look.cite: Bernard of Clairvaux, In Praise of the New Knighthood (De laude novae militiae), c. 1130s
look.prompt: Bernard was a supporter of the Templars. How might that change the way he described them?

check.q: Who was Bernard of Clairvaux?
choices: A famous monk who praised the Templars
check.why: Bernard was one of the most famous monks in Europe. He wrote in praise of the Templars.

check.q: What did Bernard say made the Templars a new kind of knight?
choices: They fought to protect others and lived simple, holy lives
check.why: Bernard said they fought to protect others and lived simple, holy lives.

check.q: How did Bernard's letter help the Templars?
choices: It found them new members and gifts
check.why: The reading says Bernard's praise helped the Templars find new members and gifts.

lessons.title: A Critic Speaks Up
lessons.mainIdea: Some people, like William of Tyre, later said the Templars had grown too proud and too rich.
reading: Not everyone praised the Templars. As the order grew rich, some people grew uneasy. One of them was William of Tyre, the archbishop who wrote the history we read before.

William said the Templars began humble and poor. But he wrote that later they became proud. He complained that they did not obey the bishops of the Holy Land. The pope had let them answer to him alone, not to local bishops. That made some church leaders angry.

A *critic* is a person who points out what he thinks is wrong. Bernard was a supporter. William was a critic. To understand the Templars, historians read both. Each one saw part of the story from his own place.

words.d: a person who points out what he or she thinks is wrong
not proud; not thinking you are better than others

look.title: Two Writers, Side by Side
look.text: Writer A, Bernard (1130s): The Templars live plainly. They obey. They protect others. Writer B, William of Tyre (1170s-1180s): The Templars began humble. Now they are proud and rich. They do not obey the bishops here.
look.prompt: The two writers lived about 40 years apart. How could both be telling part of the truth?

check.q: What is a critic?
choices: A person who keeps money safe
A person who writes a Rule
A person who points out what he thinks is wrong
check.why: A critic is a person who points out what he or she thinks is wrong.

check.q: What did William of Tyre complain about?
choices: The Templars had grown proud and did not obey local bishops
check.why: William wrote that the Templars grew proud and did not obey the bishops of the Holy Land.

check.q: Why do historians read both Bernard and William?
choices: Each saw part of the story from his own place
Only one of them could read
check.why: Bernard was a supporter and William was a critic. Reading both gives a fuller picture.

review.q: What job did the first Templars promise to do?
choices: Guard pilgrims on the roads to Jerusalem
review.why: Hugh of Payns and his friends promised to guard pilgrims on the roads.

review.q: About when did the Templars begin?
review.why: Most historians think the Templars began in 1119 or early 1120.

review.q: The Templars were both monks and knights. What does that mean?
choices: They lived by religious rules and also fought
They sailed ships and sold wool
review.why: They made monks' promises and lived by a Rule, and they also rode to battle.

review.q: Which describes a Templar knight's clothes?
choices: A black robe with a gold star
A white mantle with a red cross
A red cloak with a white lion
review.why: Templar knights wore white mantles. In the 1140s they added a red cross.

review.q: How did the Templars become rich?
choices: People gave them land, farms and money
review.why: Kings, nobles and farmers gave the Templars land, farms, mills and money.

review.q: Which was an early kind of banking the Templars did?
choices: Keeping deposits safe and moving money between houses
review.why: The Templars kept deposits safe and helped transfer money over long distances.

review.q: How are Bernard of Clairvaux and William of Tyre different?
choices: Bernard was a critic and William was a supporter
Bernard praised the Templars and William criticized them
Neither one wrote about the Templars
review.why: Bernard praised the new knights. Later, William said they had grown proud and rich.

review.q: Which Templar building can you still visit in London?
choices: The palace on the Temple Mount
review.why: The Temple Church in London was blessed in 1185 and still stands.

chapters.title: Arrested on a Friday
chapters.bigQuestion: How do historians use old records to sort what really happened to the Templars from the legends told later?

story.title: The Parchment in the Wrong Place
story.kicker: In 2001, a historian in the Vatican finds a parchment that had been out of sight for hundreds of years.
paragraphs: It is September 2001, in Vatican City, inside Rome. Barbara Frale is a historian from Italy. She works in the Vatican's archive, a huge library of old papers kept by the popes. Shelves of boxes stretch down long, quiet halls.
Frale studies very old handwriting. She is looking for papers about the Knights Templar. She opens a box and unfolds a large, pale sheet of parchment. The ink is brown with age.

She reads the Latin slowly. The parchment is dated August 1308. It says three cardinals, sent by the pope, questioned the Templar leaders at a castle called Chinon. Frale's heart beats faster. This paper had been filed in the wrong place. An old list described it too vaguely for anyone to find it.

For about 700 years, almost no one had read it. Now it could help answer an old question. What did the pope really think about the Templars? In this chapter, you will see why this piece of parchment matters, and also what it cannot prove.
story.think: Why might an important paper stay lost for hundreds of years, even inside a library?

lessons.title: Hard Times for the Templars
lessons.mainIdea: After losing the city of Acre in 1291, the Templars had lost their home base, and the king of France wanted money.
reading: In 1291, the city of Acre fell to a Muslim army. Acre was the last big Christian city in the Holy Land. The Templars lost their main home there. They moved their headquarters to the island of Cyprus.

Now some people asked a hard question. The Templars had been made to guard the Holy Land. If they could not do that, why did they still need so much land and money? The Templars still had many rich houses in Europe.

King Philip IV ruled France. He needed a lot of money for wars. He had already taken wealth from other groups in France. Many historians think he wanted the Templars' wealth and power too. Philip said he acted because he believed they had done wrong.

words.d: the main place where a group's leaders work
a large amount of money, land or valuable things

look.title: Why Would a King Act?
look.text: Here are three facts. One: the Templars lost their base in the Holy Land in 1291. Two: the Templars still owned many rich houses in France. Three: King Philip IV needed money for wars.
look.prompt: Put these facts together. What reasons might Philip have had to turn against the Templars? Which fact seems most important to you?

check.q: What happened at Acre in 1291?
choices: The city fell and the Templars lost their main home there
check.why: Acre fell in 1291. The Templars lost their main home in the Holy Land.

check.q: Who was Philip IV?
check.why: The reading says King Philip IV ruled France.

check.q: What do many historians think Philip wanted?
check.why: Many historians think Philip wanted the Templars' wealth and power.

lessons.title: Sealed Orders, Dawn Arrests
lessons.mainIdea: Philip sent secret orders on 14 September 1307, and the Templars in France were arrested at dawn on Friday, 13 October 1307.
reading: On 14 September 1307, Philip sent out letters to his officers all over France. The letters were sealed with wax. The officers were told to keep the plan secret until the right day.

The letters said terrible things about the Templars. They used strong words like horrible and bitter. These words made readers feel angry and afraid. Some words are chosen to stir up feelings. They are called *loaded words*. They can push people to believe before they see proof.

At dawn on Friday, 13 October 1307, officers knocked on the doors of Templar houses across France. They did it all at once. That way, no one could warn the others. Most of the men *arrested* were older brothers who ran farms, not young warriors.

words.d: words chosen to stir up strong feelings, so people believe something before seeing proof
taken and held by officers of the law

look.title: The King's Order Begins
look.text: The king's letter opens with a long pile of words. It calls the matter bitter, sad, horrible to think about, and terrible to hear. It calls it a hateful crime and an evil work, almost too wicked to be human.
look.cite: Philip IV of France, arrest order of 14 September 1307, English translation in Malcolm Barber, The Trial of the Templars (Cambridge University Press, 2nd ed. 2006)
look.prompt: Find the loaded words. How do they want the reader to feel? Does the opening show any proof?

check.q: On what day were the Templars in France arrested?
check.why: The arrests happened at dawn on Friday, 13 October 1307.

check.q: Why did the officers arrest the Templars all at once?
choices: So no one could warn the others
Because the pope asked them to wait
check.why: Doing it all at once meant no one could warn the others.

check.q: What are loaded words?
choices: Words that are hard to spell
Words chosen to stir up strong feelings before proof is shown
check.why: Loaded words are chosen to stir up feelings so people believe before seeing proof.

lessons.title: Forced to Confess
lessons.mainIdea: Many Templars confessed after harsh questioning, and many later took their confessions back.
reading: The king's men said the Templars had insulted the cross and turned away from Christ. They also said the Templars prayed to a strange idol. Each one is called a *charge*. A charge is a claim that someone did something wrong.

The prisoners were questioned harshly. Some were hurt. Many were frightened and alone. Frightened people often say what questioners want to hear. Many Templars chose to *confess*. That means they said they were guilty.

The leader of the Templars, called the Grand Master, was Jacques de Molay. In October 1307, he confessed to some charges. Later he took his confession back. Many others did the same. Historians still argue about how much of the charges was true. Many think the worst charges were made up.

words.d: a claim that someone did something wrong
to say that you did something wrong
the top leader of the Knights Templar

look.title: Is This Good Evidence?
look.text: Imagine a boy who is kept in a room for many hours. Adults shout at him again and again. They say, 'Just admit you broke the window.' At last he says, 'Fine, I did it.' The next day, feeling safe, he says, 'I only said that so they would stop.'
look.prompt: Is the boy's first answer strong evidence? What would you want to find before deciding what really happened?

check.q: What is a charge?
choices: A claim that someone did something wrong
check.why: A charge is a claim that someone did something wrong.

check.q: Who was Jacques de Molay?
choices: The Grand Master of the Templars
check.why: Jacques de Molay was the Grand Master, the top leader of the Templars.

check.q: Why do historians doubt many of the confessions?
choices: They came after harsh questioning, and many were taken back
The Templars wrote them as jokes
check.why: Many confessions came after harsh questioning, and many Templars later took them back.

lessons.title: Voices in the Records
lessons.mainIdea: Written records of the questioning survive, and they let us hear the words of ordinary Templar brothers.
reading: From 1309 to 1311, a group sent by the pope met in Paris. It is called the papal *commission*. It heard about 231 Templar brothers. Clerks wrote down what they said in Latin.

These pages were kept for hundreds of years. In the 1800s, a French historian named Jules Michelet printed them in two big books. They came out between 1841 and 1851. Today anyone can read them free online.

The records are full of real voices. Many speakers were not famous knights. They were farm managers, servants and cooks. A *record* like this is a *primary source*: something made at the time by people who were there.

words.d: a group of people chosen to look into something
something written down to show what happened
something made at the time by people who were there

look.title: Brothers Who Spoke
rows: Brothers heard by the pope's commission in Paris
look.cite: Jules Michelet (ed.), Procès des Templiers, 2 vols. (Paris, 1841-1851)
look.prompt: About how many brothers did the commission hear? Why might it help to have so many voices, and not just one?

check.q: About how many Templar brothers did the papal commission hear?
check.why: The papal commission in Paris heard about 231 brothers.

check.q: Who printed the commission's records in the 1800s?
check.why: Jules Michelet printed the records in two books from 1841 to 1851.

check.q: What is a primary source?
choices: Something made at the time by people who were there
The first page of any book
check.why: A primary source is made at the time by people who were there, like the commission's records.

lessons.title: Three Cardinals at a Castle
lessons.mainIdea: In August 1308, three cardinals sent by Pope Clement V questioned Templar leaders at Chinon Castle and forgave them.
reading: Pope Clement V was the head of the Catholic Church. He was French, and he lived in France, not Rome. King Philip pushed him hard to act against the Templars.
In August 1308, the pope sent three cardinals to Chinon Castle in France. A *cardinal* is a high leader in the Catholic Church. There they questioned Jacques de Molay and other Templar leaders.

The leaders asked to be forgiven. The cardinals gave them *absolution*. That means they forgave them for their sins in the name of the Church. The cardinals let them take part in church services again. They wrote all of this on a large parchment.

words.d: a high leader in the Catholic Church, just below the pope
forgiveness of sins given by a church leader

look.title: What the Parchment Says
look.text: The three cardinals wrote that the Templar leaders had asked for mercy. After hearing them, the cardinals granted them absolution. They said the leaders could return to the sacraments of the Church.
look.cite: The Chinon Parchment, 17-20 August 1308, Vatican Apostolic Archive (Archivum Arcis, Armarium D 217)
look.prompt: The cardinals forgave the leaders. Does that mean the pope thought the whole order was innocent? What else would you want to know?

check.q: Who was Clement V?
check.why: Clement V was the pope, the head of the Catholic Church.

check.q: What did the cardinals give the Templar leaders at Chinon?
check.why: The cardinals gave the leaders absolution, which is forgiveness of sins.

check.q: Where did the cardinals meet the Templar leaders in 1308?
check.why: The cardinals questioned the leaders at Chinon Castle in France.

lessons.title: Found in 2001
lessons.mainIdea: Barbara Frale found the Chinon Parchment in the Vatican's archive in 2001, after it had been misfiled for centuries.
reading: An *archive* is a place that keeps old papers and records safe. The Vatican has one of the biggest archives in the world. It holds papers from many centuries.
The Chinon Parchment was in that archive all along. But it was in the wrong place. An old list described it too vaguely to find. So it was *misfiled*, and almost no one read it.

In September 2001, the historian Barbara Frale found it. She could read the old Latin handwriting. In 2007, the Vatican helped print an exact copy of the Templar trial papers. Only 799 numbered copies were made. One of them is in the Law Library of Congress, in Washington, D.C.

words.d: a place that keeps old papers and records safe
put in the wrong place, so it is hard to find
a writing material made from animal skin, used long ago

look.title: A Long Wait
rows: Printed copy of the trial papers
look.cite: Vatican Secret Archives, Processus contra Templarios (Scrinium, 2007); Library of Congress Law Library blog, Templar Secrets at the Law Library of Congress (2011)
look.prompt: About how many years passed between writing the parchment and finding it again?

check.q: What is an archive?
choices: A place that keeps old papers and records safe
check.why: An archive is a place that keeps old papers and records safe.

check.q: Why was the Chinon Parchment hard to find?
choices: It was buried in the ground
It was misfiled and described too vaguely
check.why: The parchment was misfiled, and an old list described it too vaguely.

check.q: Where in the United States can you find one of the 799 printed copies?
check.why: One of the 799 numbered copies is in the Law Library of Congress in Washington, D.C.

lessons.title: What the Parchment Proves
lessons.mainIdea: The parchment shows the leaders were forgiven in 1308, but it does not prove the pope declared the whole order innocent.
reading: When news of the find came out, some headlines said the pope had found the Templars innocent. That went further than the parchment. The parchment says the cardinals forgave certain leaders. It did not end the trials.

Frale thinks Pope Clement wanted to fix the order, not destroy it. She thinks the king's pressure was too strong for him. Many historians agree with parts of her view. Others are more careful. This is a question historians still *debate*.

A good reader asks two questions. What does the document really say? And what are people claiming it says? The distance between those answers is where mistakes can grow. Checking the *evidence* yourself helps you see clearly.

words.d: to discuss a question when people have different views
facts or objects that help show whether something is true

look.title: Headline or Document?
look.text: Headline: Old Paper Proves Templars Were Innocent! Document: Three cardinals forgave Jacques de Molay and some other leaders, and let them back into church services, in August 1308.
look.prompt: How is the headline different from the document? Rewrite the headline so it matches the evidence.

check.q: What does the Chinon Parchment show?
choices: The cardinals forgave certain Templar leaders in 1308
The pope declared every Templar innocent
check.why: The parchment records that the cardinals forgave certain leaders. It did not end the trials.

check.q: What does Barbara Frale think Pope Clement wanted?
choices: To fix the order, not destroy it
check.why: Frale thinks Clement wanted to reform the order but gave in to the king's pressure.

check.q: What does debate mean?
choices: To discuss a question when people have different views
check.why: To debate is to discuss a question when people have different views.

lessons.title: The Pope Ends the Order
lessons.mainIdea: In 1312, Pope Clement V ended the Templar order without ever declaring it guilty, and most of its land went to the Hospitallers.
reading: From 1311 to 1312, church leaders met at the Council of Vienne, in France. On 22 March 1312, Pope Clement V ended the Templar order. He chose to *suppress* it. That means he shut it down for good.
But the pope did not say the order was guilty. He said he was ending it by his own power as pope, not by a court's judgment. So the Templars were never found guilty as a whole group.

In May 1312, the pope gave most Templar lands to another order of knights, the *Hospitallers*. In Portugal, the king started a new group in 1319, with the pope's approval. It was called the Order of Christ, and it took over the Templar lands there. Some brothers joined it.

words.d: to shut something down by force or by order
another religious order of knights; it got most of the Templars' land in 1312

look.title: The Pope's Decision
look.text: The pope wrote that he was ending the Order of the Temple. He said he did this by his power as pope, not by a final court sentence. He forbade anyone to join the order or to wear its clothes from then on.
look.cite: Pope Clement V, Vox in excelso, Council of Vienne, 22 March 1312 (English in N. P. Tanner, ed., Decrees of the Ecumenical Councils, 1990)
look.prompt: The pope ended the order but did not call it guilty. Why might he have chosen to do it this way?

check.q: When did Pope Clement V end the Templar order?
check.why: Clement V suppressed the order on 22 March 1312, at the Council of Vienne.

check.q: Did the pope declare the order guilty?
choices: No, he ended it by his own power without a guilty verdict
No, because the king stopped him
check.why: The pope ended the order by his power as pope, not by a court's judgment.

check.q: Who got most of the Templars' land?
check.why: In May 1312, the pope gave most Templar lands to the Hospitallers.

lessons.title: The Last Grand Master
lessons.mainIdea: Jacques de Molay was put to death in Paris on 18 March 1314, and a legend of a curse grew up later.
reading: Jacques de Molay was held in prison for about seven years. In March 1314, he spoke out in public. He said the order was holy and the charges were false. For this, he and another leader, Geoffroi de Charney, were put to death by fire. It happened on 18 March 1314, on a small island in Paris.

A writer from that time said Molay called on God to set things right. Later, the story grew bigger. People said Molay cursed the pope and the king. They said both would die within a year. This is a *legend*, a story told often that may not be true.

Here is a fact that helped the legend grow. Pope Clement died in April 1314. King Philip died in November 1314. Both died that year. But the full curse story was written down years later. The first writer does not record it.

words.d: a story told often that may or may not be true
words that wish something bad on someone

look.title: The Year 1314
rows: Jacques de Molay put to death
look.cite: Malcolm Barber, The Trial of the Templars (Cambridge University Press, 2nd ed. 2006)
look.prompt: Put the three events in order. How could these dates make people believe in a curse, even without proof?

check.q: When was Jacques de Molay put to death?
check.why: Molay and Geoffroi de Charney were put to death on 18 March 1314 in Paris.

check.q: What is a legend?
choices: A story told often that may not be true
check.why: A legend is a story told often that may or may not be true.

check.q: What fact helped the curse legend grow?
choices: The pope and the king both died later in 1314
check.why: Clement died in April 1314 and Philip in November 1314, which made the curse story seem true.

lessons.title: Friday the 13th and Hidden Treasure
lessons.mainIdea: Stories about Templar treasure and bad-luck Friday the 13th are not backed by evidence from the time.
reading: Many people say Friday the 13th is unlucky because of the Templar arrests. The arrest date is real. But written fears about Friday the 13th show up in the 1800s. A 1907 novel called Friday, the Thirteenth helped spread the idea. The Templar link was added even later.

Other stories say the Templars hid a great *treasure* before the arrests. Some say ships sailed away with gold. Historians have looked hard through the trial records. They have found no solid proof of a treasure fleet.

No Templar treasure has ever been found. People have searched castles, churches and islands. A story can be exciting and still have no *proof*. Historians say what the evidence shows, and they name a legend as a legend.

words.d: gold, jewels or other valuable things, often hidden
evidence strong enough to show that something is true

look.title: Sort the Claims
look.text: Claim 1: The Templars were arrested on Friday, 13 October 1307. Claim 2: The arrests are why Friday the 13th is unlucky. Claim 3: Templar ships carried away a huge treasure that is still hidden today.
look.prompt: Which claim is backed by records from the time? Which ones are legends? Tell what clue helped you decide.

check.q: Which part of the Friday the 13th story is backed by records?
choices: The Templar arrests really happened on Friday, 13 October 1307
The pope named the day unlucky
check.why: The arrest date is documented. The bad-luck link came much later.

check.q: Has any Templar treasure ever been found?
choices: No, none has ever been found
check.why: The reading says no Templar treasure has ever been found.

check.q: What is proof?
choices: Evidence strong enough to show something is true
A guess made in a novel
check.why: Proof is evidence strong enough to show that something is true.

lessons.title: Did They Secretly Survive?
lessons.mainIdea: Some later groups borrowed the Templar name, but no record shows the medieval order secretly lived on.
reading: Some people say the Templars did not really end. They say the knights hid. Later, they say, the knights became the Freemasons, a brotherhood that grew out of the lodges of stonemasons. But the first written link between Masons and crusading knights shows up in 1737. Claims about the Templars came in the 1750s. That is more than 400 years after 1312. No record from the Templars' time links the two groups.

Later, some Masonic groups named themselves Knights Templar. In 1880, thousands of these American Knights Templar met in Chicago. They camped in tents by Lake Michigan and wore plumed hats. They even printed their own daily newspaper for the event.

These Chicago knights admired the old Templars. They were *inspired by* them. But they were not *descended from* them. That means no line of members runs back to the medieval order. Knowing that difference is a big part of thinking like a historian.

words.d: getting ideas from someone or something you admire
coming in an unbroken line from an earlier person or group

look.title: Same Name, Different Group
look.text: Your school has a team called the Knights. Their shirts have a shield and a sword. Five hundred years ago, real knights rode horses in Europe. Your school team took the name because they like knights.
look.prompt: Is your school team descended from real knights, or inspired by them? How is this like the Chicago Knights Templar of 1880?

check.q: When does the first written link between Freemasons and crusading knights appear?
check.why: The first written link shows up in 1737, more than 400 years after the order ended.

check.q: What happened in Chicago in 1880?
choices: The medieval Templars were found hiding
Thousands of American Masonic Knights Templar met there
check.why: In 1880, thousands of American Masonic Knights Templar met in Chicago by Lake Michigan.

check.q: What is the difference between inspired by and descended from?
choices: Descended from means admiring; inspired by means related
Inspired by means taking ideas; descended from means an unbroken line
Both mean being in the same family
check.why: Inspired by means getting ideas from something you admire. Descended from means an unbroken line.

review.q: Which king had the Templars in France arrested?
review.why: King Philip IV of France had the Templars arrested in 1307.

review.q: Why do historians doubt many Templar confessions?
choices: They were given after harsh questioning and many were taken back
review.why: Many confessions came after harsh questioning, and many Templars later took them back.

review.q: What did the Chinon Parchment record?
choices: Three cardinals forgiving Templar leaders in 1308
review.why: The parchment records that three cardinals gave the leaders absolution at Chinon in 1308.

review.q: Who found the Chinon Parchment, and when?
review.why: Historian Barbara Frale found it in the Vatican's archive in 2001.

review.q: How did the pope end the Templar order in 1312?
choices: By a court that found them guilty
By asking the Templars to vote
By his own power, without a guilty verdict
review.why: The pope ended the order by his own power, not by a court's judgment.

review.q: Which statement is a legend, not a documented fact?
choices: The Templars were arrested on 13 October 1307
Molay was put to death in March 1314
Molay's curse made the king and pope die
The pope ended the order in 1312
review.why: The curse story was written down years later. The others are documented.

review.q: How is the Chinon Parchment different from the treasure stories?
choices: The parchment is a real record from the time; the treasure stories have no proof
The treasure was found, but the parchment was lost
review.why: The parchment is a primary source from 1308. No evidence backs the treasure stories.

choices: the same group as the medieval Templars
review.why: They admired and borrowed from the old order, but no line of members links them.
